meta.description: Seven-chapter financial accounting curriculum for FinanceLab. Each chapter has one pre-generated reading session (~30 min) followed by examples and a quiz.

sessions.title: The Accounting Framework & Financial Statements
learningObjectives: Explain why accounting is called the 'language of business' and who uses financial reports
Identify the three core financial statements and what question each answers
Apply the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity) and explain why it always holds
Explain the rules of double-entry bookkeeping and the debit/credit logic
Distinguish between revenue recognition (earned, not collected) and the matching principle
Read a functional (multi-step) income statement and identify EBIT and gross margin
keyConcepts: Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
Balance Sheet, Income Statement, Statement of Cash Flows
Double-entry bookkeeping: debits = credits always
Revenue recognition: earned, not when cash received
Matching principle: expenses matched to revenues in the same period
Accrual vs. cash-basis accounting
EBIT and gross margin
coreFormulasForLibrary: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
Net Income = Revenues − Expenses
Gross Profit = Net Sales − COGS
EBIT = Net Sales − COGS − SG&A
quizTopics: Multiple choice: identify which financial statement answers a given question
Short answer: explain what happens to each of the three statements when a credit sale is made
Fill-in-the-blank: complete a simple multi-step income statement and identify EBIT
Short answer: explain the difference between accrual and cash-basis accounting
sessions.analystNote: Every PE/IB interview starts with the accounting equation. Know it cold and be able to walk through what happens to all three statements when a transaction occurs.

sessions.title: Inventory
learningObjectives: Identify the three types of inventory (raw materials, WIP, finished goods) and trace costs through the manufacturing cycle
Explain the three cost flow assumptions: FIFO, LIFO, and Weighted Average Cost
Analyse the income statement and balance sheet effects of each cost method under inflation
Understand why LIFO is forbidden under IFRS and allowed under US GAAP
Use the LIFO reserve to restate LIFO financials to FIFO for comparability
Apply the lower of cost and NRV rule (IAS 2) and explain how write-downs flow through COGS
keyConcepts: Raw materials → WIP → Finished goods cost flow
FIFO: first in, first out — lower COGS in inflation, higher gross profit
LIFO: last in, first out — higher COGS in inflation, lower gross profit (US GAAP only)
Weighted Average Cost: smooths price fluctuations
LIFO reserve: cumulative balance sheet distortion
LIFO liquidation: manipulation risk when old cheap layers are depleted
Lower of cost and NRV: IAS 2 write-down rule
coreFormulasForLibrary: COGS = Beginning Inventory + Purchases − Ending Inventory
LIFO Reserve = FIFO Inventory − LIFO Inventory
Inventory Days = (Inventory / COGS) × 365
NRV = Estimated Selling Price − Costs to Complete and Sell
quizTopics: Multiple choice: which cost method produces the highest net income under rising prices?
Fill-in-the-blank: given unit costs and quantities, compute COGS and ending inventory under FIFO and weighted average
Short answer: explain the LIFO reserve and how to use it to adjust a LIFO firm's balance sheet
Short answer: what is LIFO liquidation and why does it inflate reported profits?
sessions.analystNote: In due diligence, always check the inventory accounting note. LIFO firms need to be restated to FIFO for comparability. Watch inventory/sales ratios — rising inventory days can signal demand problems or channel stuffing.

sessions.title: Accounts Receivable
learningObjectives: Explain why accounts receivable arises and how it is reported at net realizable value
Distinguish the direct write-off method from the allowance method and explain why IFRS requires the latter
Apply the income statement approach (% of credit sales) and the balance sheet approach (aging) to estimate bad debt expense
Journal the full allowance method cycle: year-end estimate, actual write-off, and recovery
Calculate Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) and interpret what rising DSO signals
Identify earnings management red flags in accounts receivable
keyConcepts: Net realizable value = Gross AR − Allowance for Uncollectible Accounts (AUA)
AUA is a contra-asset, not a liability
Allowance method: matches bad debt expense to the revenue period
Aging of receivables: preferred balance sheet approach to estimating AUA
Write-offs under allowance method: no P&L effect — reduce both gross AR and AUA
DSO = (AR / Net Sales) × 365
Rising DSO: revenue quality or collection red flag
coreFormulasForLibrary: Net AR = Gross AR − Allowance for Uncollectible Accounts
DSO = (Accounts Receivable / Net Sales) × 365
Bad Debt Expense = % of Credit Sales × Credit Sales (income statement approach)
AUA Adjustment = Target AUA Balance − Current AUA Balance (aging approach)
quizTopics: Multiple choice: what is the effect on net AR when an account is written off under the allowance method?
Fill-in-the-blank: given aging schedule percentages and balances, compute the required AUA balance and bad debt expense
Short answer: explain why the direct write-off method violates the matching principle
Short answer: a company's revenue grew 10% but AR grew 25% — what questions would you ask?
sessions.analystNote: DSO and AUA coverage are two of the first things you check in a quality of earnings review. Receivables that grow faster than revenue or an AUA that shrinks relative to gross AR are classic earnings management signals.

sessions.title: The Statement of Cash Flows
learningObjectives: Explain why net income and operating cash flow diverge under accrual accounting
Identify and classify transactions into CFO, CFI, and CFF
Construct CFO using the indirect method: start from net income, adjust for non-cash items and working capital changes
Understand IFRS flexibility vs. US GAAP rules on interest and dividend classification
Calculate Free Cash Flow (FCF) and explain why it — not net income — drives valuation
Use the Cash Realization Ratio to assess earnings quality
keyConcepts: CFO: cash from core operations — most important section
CFI: cash from long-term asset transactions (CapEx, acquisitions)
CFF: cash from capital raising and return (debt, equity, dividends)
Indirect method: Net Income + D&A − ΔWorking Capital Assets + ΔWorking Capital Liabilities
Free Cash Flow = CFO − CapEx
Cash Realization Ratio = CFO / Net Income
Cash flow lifecycle: startup (CFO−, CFF+), mature (CFO+, CFF−), declining (CFI+)
coreFormulasForLibrary: Free Cash Flow (FCF) = CFO − CapEx
Cash Realization Ratio = CFO / Net Income
CFO (indirect) = Net Income + Depreciation − ΔAR − ΔInventory + ΔAP + ΔAccrued Liabilities
quizTopics: Multiple choice: classify a given transaction into CFO, CFI, or CFF
Fill-in-the-blank: given an income statement and balance sheet changes, build the CFO section using the indirect method
Short answer: a company has $50M net income but $10M CFO — what are three possible explanations?
Short answer: explain why FCF rather than net income is the correct input for LBO and DCF models
sessions.analystNote: In LBO and DCF models, you're discounting free cash flow, not earnings. Always reconcile net income to CFO — the gap tells you whether profits are cash-backed. A sustained Cash Realization Ratio below 1 is a major red flag.

sessions.title: Measuring Performance
learningObjectives: Perform common-size analysis on income statements and balance sheets
Explain operating leverage and calculate its effect on profit under different revenue scenarios
Calculate and interpret efficiency ratios: inventory days, DSO, DPO, CCC, asset turnover
Calculate and interpret financial strength ratios: current ratio, debt ratio, interest coverage
Calculate and interpret profitability ratios: gross margin, EBIT margin, ROA, ROE
Decompose ROE using the DuPont framework: margin × asset turnover × leverage
Identify earnings quality red flags: aggressive revenue recognition, cookie jar reserves, D&A gaming
keyConcepts: Common-size analysis: all IS items as % of revenue, BS items as % of total assets
Operating leverage: high fixed costs → profits more sensitive to revenue changes
Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) = Inventory Days + DSO − DPO
DuPont decomposition: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier
EBITDA normalization: add back non-recurring items before applying multiples
Earnings quality: how faithfully net income represents sustainable, cash-backed performance
coreFormulasForLibrary: CCC = Inventory Days + DSO − DPO
ROE = Net Income / Equity = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier (DuPont)
ROA = Net Income / Total Assets
Interest Coverage = EBIT / Interest Expense
Debt Ratio = Total Debt / Total Assets
Asset Turnover = Revenue / Total Assets
quizTopics: Multiple choice: a company has the same ROE as a peer — what does DuPont analysis reveal about how each achieves it?
Fill-in-the-blank: given financial data, calculate CCC and interpret what a negative CCC means
Short answer: explain the difference between EBITDA and free cash flow, and when each is more useful
Short answer: list four earnings quality red flags and explain why each is a concern
sessions.analystNote: Before applying any valuation multiple, normalize EBITDA. In models, always stress-test operating leverage — a 10% revenue decline can destroy 30–50% of EBIT for a high-fixed-cost business.

sessions.title: Minority Interest & Consolidation
learningObjectives: Explain when and why a parent company consolidates a subsidiary (>50% ownership)
Calculate goodwill using both the partial goodwill (book value MI) and full goodwill (market value MI) methods
Understand the difference between partial and full goodwill under IFRS 3
Explain why goodwill is not amortized under IFRS but is tested annually for impairment
Deduct minority interest correctly in the equity value bridge: EV − Net Debt − MI = Equity Value
Explain why EBITDA multiples must be applied to fully consolidated EBITDA and MI subtracted separately
keyConcepts: Consolidation: 100% of subsidiary assets/liabilities on parent's balance sheet when >50% owned
Minority interest (NCI): portion of subsidiary equity not owned by parent — sits within equity
Goodwill = Purchase Price − Fair Value of Net Identifiable Assets
Partial goodwill method: MI measured at book value of net assets
Full goodwill method: MI measured at implied market value of 100%
Goodwill impairment: one-way, cannot be reversed under IFRS
Equity bridge: EV − Net Debt − Minority Interest = Equity Value to parent
coreFormulasForLibrary: Goodwill = Purchase Price − (Fair Value of Net Identifiable Assets × % Acquired)
Equity Value = EV − Net Debt − Minority Interest
Full Goodwill MI = % minority × Implied 100% MV of subsidiary
Partial Goodwill MI = % minority × Book Value of Net Assets
quizTopics: Multiple choice: a parent acquires 70% of a subsidiary — how is the remaining 30% shown on the consolidated balance sheet?
Fill-in-the-blank: given purchase price, fair value of net assets, and ownership %, calculate goodwill under both partial and full goodwill methods
Short answer: why does failing to subtract minority interest overstate equity value in an M&A model?
Short answer: explain what goodwill impairment tells you about whether a deal thesis is working
sessions.analystNote: In any deal with a partially-owned subsidiary, the minority interest deduction in the equity bridge is non-negotiable. Forgetting it is a classic interview mistake. EV/EBITDA multiples capture 100% of the business — MI must come out before you get to equity value.

sessions.title: Mergers & Acquisitions
learningObjectives: Identify the main motivations for M&A transactions and explain how synergies justify the acquisition premium
Apply IFRS 3 acquisition accounting: PPA, recognition of off-balance-sheet intangibles, and goodwill calculation
Explain the post-acquisition income statement impact of PPA: D&A step-up on acquired intangibles and PPE
Understand bargain purchases (negative goodwill) and how they are recognized
Identify intercompany eliminations required in consolidation
Evaluate a deal using EPS accretion/dilution analysis alongside EBITDA multiples
keyConcepts: Acquisition premium: buyer's public commitment to the value creation thesis
Purchase Price Allocation (PPA): revalue all assets/liabilities at fair value at acquisition date
Off-balance-sheet intangibles: brands, customer relationships, technology — recognized for first time in PPA
Goodwill = Purchase Price − Fair Value of Net Identifiable Assets (residual)
PPA step-up: higher D&A post-acquisition reduces reported net income but not EBITDA
Bargain purchase: negative goodwill — recognized as gain in P&L on acquisition date
Intercompany eliminations: loans, sales, investment account must be removed in consolidation
coreFormulasForLibrary: Goodwill = Purchase Price − Fair Value of Net Identifiable Assets
Acquisition Premium = (Deal Price − Pre-Deal Share Price) / Pre-Deal Share Price
EPS Accretion/Dilution = (Pro Forma EPS − Standalone EPS) / Standalone EPS
Post-Acquisition D&A Add-back = Acquired Intangibles / Useful Life + Step-up Depreciation
quizTopics: Multiple choice: a company acquires a target and pays $50M above the fair value of net assets — where does this appear on the balance sheet?
Fill-in-the-blank: given a purchase price and PPA schedule, calculate goodwill and the annual post-acquisition D&A charge
Short answer: explain why bankers use EBITDA multiples rather than P/E in M&A valuation
Short answer: what is EPS accretion/dilution analysis and why is it an insufficient deal filter on its own?
sessions.analystNote: PPA amortization add-backs in 'adjusted EPS' are legitimate but should be scrutinized. Synergies are consistently overestimated — always model a downside case. Goodwill impairment in subsequent years is often the first public signal that a deal thesis has failed.
